title: Apple Doing Well in China, But Facing Challenges, But It's OK, Says Morgan Stanley - Barron's

https://www.barrons.com/articles/apple-doing-well-in-china-but-facing-challenges-but-its-okay-says-morgan-stanley-1518725031 Apple Doing Well in China, But Facing Challenges, But It’s OK, Says Morgan Stanley By Feb. 15, 2018 3:03 p.m. ET Text Size Medium Large 
You might need a PlayBill to follow the action in China for Apple ’s ( AAPL ) iPhone X, so complicated are the puts and takes, as laid out today by Morgan Stanley ’s Katy Huberty . 
Basically, the company’s been gobbling share, but how much it can gobble is somewhat constrained because the Chinese are holding on to phones longer, and competitors are undercutting older iPhones. 
Huberty, who has an Overweight rating on Apple stock, and a $203 price target, reviews data from a firm called Jiguang , which makes a practice of aggregating such stuff. 
Apple, as previously reported , topped worldwide sales in Q4, the December quarter, helped by the iPhone X , even as sales in China dropped, year over year, for the first time on record. Apple’s gains came despite gains by its small, local rivals, including Oppo and Xiaomi . 
But the number of phones Apple in that quarter, 77.3 million, was below Street consensus, so Huberty takes a look at what’s happening. 
The Jiguang data shows Apple had a rising share of shipments in Q4, at almost 22% of the “active smartphone base in China,” but that share “ticked down” in January, while that of local brands ticked up from their Q4 level, she writes. 
So, Apple’s had its biggest-ever decline from one period to the next in the month of January, at the hands of these local brands: 
iPhone had 20.6% share of the active smartphone market in China in the 4 week period ending January 14th, 2018, down from 21.8% in the prior 4 week period ending December 31, 2017. This represents the second largest period over period share loss since we began tracking this data in January 2017 (largest was in August 2017), with market share largely picked up by the big 4 Chinese smartphone vendors. 
Huberty concludes that owners of Android phones are “ switching ” to an iPhone less frequently because they’re holding onto phones longer. She writes, "Android replacement cycles elongated despite iPhone replacement cycles shrinking in 4Q17, which reduced the switcher opportunity […] compared to our bottom-up model." 
As a result, all the competitive action was in the "the mid-market” — less pricey models, concludes Huberty. 
And there, Apple’s older phones, like the iPhone 6 and 7, lost share as the local brands go after Apple with cheaper offerings. 
"Apple selling iPhone 6 at a $350 starting point and iPhone 7/7+ $130-200 below the new iPhone 8/8+ accelerated demand for older products. However that demand seems to be fading as Chinese brands respond to significant share loss in the mid-market during 4Q17." 
She expects pricing cuts by the local brands to “intensify” as they try and clear inventory. 
But Huberty ends on a happy note . 
"A rising retention rate and a switching rate above peers shows that Apple platform share gains can still accelerate as the market matures,” she writes. 
"With over 1⁄3 of the Apple installed base in China still owning an iPhone 6 or older model compared to 20% that owned an iPhone 5S or older a year ago, there remains significant untapped potential for continued upgrades/share gains." 
All this, by the way, comes as research firm Strategy Analytics today declared that Apple for the first time ever made more than half the revenue of the overall smartphone industry in Q4. 
Apple stock today is up $5.55, or 3%, at $172.92.
